notes: Full judgment on case stated appeal from sex-establishment closure order; procedural service and notice issues resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Closure order appeal: service of summons and notice under Westminster sex-establishment legislation
key_facts: Bow Street Magistrates' Court made a closure order under section 4(6) of the City of Westminster Act 1996 in respect of premises at Peter Street and Berwick Street operating as an unlicensed sex establishment since at least May 2000.

Appellants Gonis and Girvan challenged the order on technical grounds relating to the timeliness of the complaint, service of the summons on Gonis, and whether notice of proceedings had been given to Porterre SA as registered proprietor.
A closure notice had lawfully been served on 3 September 2002; the complaint bore the date 28 February 2003 and the summons was sent by first-class post to Gonis's last known address.
Porterre SA was not a party to the proceedings and had not sought judicial review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated to the Administrative Court from Bow Street Magistrates' Court's closure order, treated as an application for judicial review.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; magistrates' decision upheld; defendant's costs ordered subject to detailed assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Under the Westminster Act closure scheme, failure to serve section 4(4) notice of hearing on a person served with a discretionary closure notice under section 3(2)(b) does not render proceedings a nullity where mandatory closure notice service under section 3(2)(a) was effective; procedural requirements using 'shall' must be read in light of statutory purpose per Mendoza. Service of a summons by first-class post to the defendant's last known address is effective under Magistrates' Courts Rules 1981 rule 99 despite non-compliance with section 8 of the 1996 Act. Personal appellants have no standing to complain of procedural failings affecting only Porterre SA.
legal_issues: Whether the closure complaint was made within six months of service of the closure notice
Whether summons service on Zaharis Gonis was effective
Whether failure to give Porterre SA notice of the hearing rendered the proceedings a nullity or required adjournment
Whether appellants could raise Porterre SA's procedural interests

linked_authorities.citation: Westminster City Council v Mendoza [2001] EWCA Civ 216
London and Clydeside Estates Ltd v Aberdeen DC [1980] 1 WLR 182

notes: Full detailed assessment judgment on solicitor fee estimates and hourly rates.

enrichment.short_title: Solicitors' bill assessment: holding firm to December costs estimate and engagement-letter rates
key_facts: Boyes Turner acted for Trevor and John Slade in Chancery litigation against Seema and Sona Builders Ltd from May 2000 until compromise on 15 February 2002, billing nearly £100,000.

Three invoices (19 February, 26 February and 20 March 2002) were referred to detailed assessment; the main dispute concerned the 19 February bill charging £11,000 profit costs and £14,250 counsel fees.

In December 2001 the solicitors estimated trial costs from that point at £20,000–£25,000 excluding VAT; a revised estimate of an additional £19,000 was communicated only on 12 February 2002, shortly before trial.
The trial settled on the second day; the Slades had not received written notice of increased hourly rates from £170/£140 to £180/£150.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment under section 70 Solicitors Act 1974 of three solicitors' bills following order dated 14 February 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Bills substantially reduced on estimate and rate grounds; 19 February bill allowed at £24,887.54; minor reductions on other bills; no order as to costs of the assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Clients must be told in clear terms if hourly rates are to increase; inference from time printouts attached to bills is insufficient (Wong v Vizards). Solicitors must inform clients as soon as it appears an estimate will or is likely to be exceeded, not after work is done. Where a revised estimate is communicated too late and clients are presented with a fait accompli, the original estimate binds, with a margin consistent with Wong and Anthony v Ellis & Fairbairn (approximately 15% above worst-case scenario). Failed rate increases revert to engagement-letter rates.
legal_issues: Whether Boyes Turner should be held to the December 2001 or February 2002 costs estimate
Whether partner and assistant hourly rates of £180 and £150 were recoverable without prior written notification
How much the Slades had paid on account
Who should bear costs of the detailed assessment under section 70(9)

linked_authorities.citation: Wong v Vizards (A Firm) [1997] 2 Costs LR 46
Anthony v Ellis & Fairbairn (A Firm) [2002] 2 Costs LR 277

notes: Full case stated judgment on EPA noise nuisance prosecution appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Noise nuisance prosecution: magistrates' acquittal on best practicable means defence quashed
key_facts: Tewkesbury Borough Council granted Mr Deacon temporary planning permission for a wedding/events tent with conditions limiting amplified music and prohibiting DJ voice transmissions.
Environmental health officers detected excessive amplified music and voice transmissions; abatement notices were served on 23 July 2002 after earlier warnings.
The notices were not appealed; further breaches led to prosecution before Gloucestershire magistrates, who acquitted Deacon and his company on eight counts.
Defendants relied solely on the statutory defence of best practicable means under section 80(7), including purchase of a sound compressor and an informal 2001 agreement allowing five DJ voice-overs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' acquittals following prosecution for breach of abatement notices under the Environmental Protection Act 1990.
enrichment.outcome: Magistrates' verdicts discharged; matter remitted with direction to convict; magistrates' costs order below also discharged; council awarded £3,835.76 costs on appeal.
enrichment.ratio: The best practicable means defence requires the defendant to have used effective means to prevent or counteract the nuisance, not merely to install equipment or seek local authority assistance in setting levels. Local authorities are not obliged to advise perpetrators how to comply with noise restrictions (R v Falmouth and Truro Port Health Authority). An informal officer agreement permitting voice-overs was superseded by the 2002 planning permission and subsequent abatement notices; ignorance of retraction is not a valid defence where planning conditions and enforcement letters put the defendant on notice.
legal_issues: Whether defendants proved best practicable means under section 80(7) EPA 1990
Whether reliance on informal agreement for DJ voice-overs justified acquittal
Whether local authority failure to advise on compressor settings supported the defence
Whether pre-1990 case law on reasonable excuse was relevant where that defence was not advanced

linked_authorities.citation: R v Falmouth and Truro Port Health Authority [2001] QB 445

notes: Full Costs Judge judgment on misconduct and delay in post-judgment costs assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Costs misconduct application dismissed where solicitor delayed assessment but charge lawfully subsisted
key_facts: Bernard Oberman & Co obtained summary judgment in 1997 against Mr Steinberg for unpaid solicitors' bills arising from a professional negligence claim against former counsel William Poulton.

Charging orders were made over Flat 11 Avenue Road and later Flat 49 Park Crescent; principal judgment debt was paid in March 1999 but costs under Master Bragge's October 1998 and January 1999 orders remained unassessed until August 2002.
Parallel libel proceedings between the parties were stayed and later resolved under the Defamation Act 1996 summary procedure with modest damages.
Steinberg applied for total disallowance of two costs bills for delay and alleged misconduct in maintaining the Flat 11 charge to stifle the libel claim.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application at Costs Judge level for total disallowance of bills arising from Chancery enforcement orders, heard together with detailed assessment on 25 September 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Misconduct application failed; interest disallowed for delay period conceded; detailed assessment of bills proceeded.
enrichment.ratio: Misconduct under CPR 44.14(1)(b) requires conduct beyond negligence, akin to abuse of process (Ridehalgh v Horsefield; Medcalf v Mardell; Persaud v Persaud). Where pre-CPR orders provided for costs to be assessed in Chambers under Order 62 rule 13 without a time limit, delay alone does not justify total disallowance; the remedy is disallowance of interest under CPR 47.8. Maintaining a charging order until assessed costs are paid, where the order expressly so provides, is not improper conduct even during parallel hostile litigation. Enforcement in New York when Land Registry searches showed no UK assets was not unreasonable.
legal_issues: Whether delay in commencing detailed assessment warranted total disallowance of costs
Whether maintaining the Flat 11 charge to pressure Steinberg in libel proceedings amounted to misconduct
Whether Mr Cohn misled Master Bragge at the 4 July 2002 hearing
Whether New York enforcement proceedings were improper

linked_authorities.citation: Ridehalgh v Horsefield [1994] Ch 205
Medcalf v Mardell [2002] 3 WLR 172
Persaud v Persaud [2003] P.N.L.R. 519
Bufton v Hill [2002] 3 Costs LR 381

notes: Full reserved Court of Appeal sentencing judgment substituting DTTO for custody.

enrichment.short_title: Drug-driven acquisitive offending: immediate custody replaced with drug treatment and testing order
key_facts: Peter Belli pleaded guilty to theft of a CD player, burglary of an unoccupied cottage (DNA match; telephone line cut), shoplifting toiletries, and failing to surrender to bail.
He had a long history of acquisitive and serious offending linked to drug use; probation and DTTO assessment reports recommended a twelve-month drug treatment and testing order.
Chester Crown Court imposed two years nine months' immediate imprisonment on 4 February 2003, rejecting a DTTO as inappropriate given offence seriousness, especially the burglary.
Further report dated 20 June 2003 showed negative drug tests in prison and strong motivation to abstain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) with leave; reasons reserved after sentence quashed at hearing on 1 September 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; sentences of imprisonment quashed; drug treatment and testing order substituted.
enrichment.ratio: A DTTO is a demanding community sentence aimed at breaking the link between drug addiction and acquisitive crime; sentencers must give proper consideration to it and must not reject it solely because custody would otherwise be appropriate or because of the scale of offending (Kelly; Robinson). Volume and type of acquisitive offending may favour a DTTO, but actual criminality remains relevant (Attorney General's Reference No 28 of 2001). Where fresh post-sentence material strongly supports treatment, the balance may decisively favour substitution even if the original sentence was arguably within discretion.
legal_issues: Whether the sentencing judge erred in rejecting a DTTO for drug-motivated acquisitive offences
How to balance offence seriousness against rehabilitation through DTTO
Whether post-sentence reports justified substituting a DTTO on appeal

enrichment.short_title: SFO judicial review: quashing magistrates' erroneous withdrawal of extradition arrest warrant
key_facts: The Serious Fraud Office investigated Charles Alistair Forsyth, former managing director of Personal Computer Sciences Ltd, in relation to alleged fraud offences after the company entered receivership in July 1999 with debts of £4–5 million.

Forsyth avoided UK interviews, fled abroad, and was arrested in Western Australia following a warrant issued on 17 October 2002 after prima facie extradition proceedings at York/Selby magistrates' court.
On 5 August 2003 Selby Magistrates' Court, during an erroneous 'rolling review' of outstanding warrants without notice to the SFO, police, or Forsyth, withdrew the case and all warrants.
Discovery of the error during pending Australian extradition proceedings led to urgent judicial review; Burton J granted interim relief preserving warrant validity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review to quash Selby Magistrates' Court's decision of 5 August 2003 withdrawing informations and arrest warrants in SFO fraud prosecution.
enrichment.outcome: Order granted quashing the withdrawal decision; warrant validity preserved pending appeal rights.
enrichment.ratio: Although section 125(1) Magistrates' Courts Act 1980 permits withdrawal of a warrant by the issuing justice, that power must be exercised only on proper information laid before the court. Withdrawal without notice to the prosecutor during an administrative 'rolling review' in a live extradition case was an improper exercise of power amenable to quashing for error of law (R v Bedwellty Justices ex p Williams). Restarting proceedings was not an acceptable alternative where it would treat the irregular withdrawal as regular and jeopardise custody in Australia.
legal_issues: Whether magistrates properly exercised power under section 125 to withdraw the arrest warrant
Whether judicial review should intervene where the decision favoured the unconvicted defendant
Whether restarting proceedings was an adequate alternative remedy
Effect of incomplete court records on the magistrates' decision

linked_authorities.citation: R v Bedwellty Justices ex parte Williams [1997] AC 225

notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on burden of proof in M25 junction road traffic collision.

enrichment.short_title: M25 junction collision: judge erred in dismissing both claim and counterclaim on burden of proof
key_facts: Mrs Cooper (82) and Mr Crompton collided while leaving the M25 at junction 10 to join the A3 northbound on 27 November 2000 in wet, greasy, heavy traffic.

They gave diametrically opposed accounts: Cooper said Crompton undertook her from the nearside lane shortly after traffic lights; Crompton said Cooper had overshot the A3 slip road and manoeuvred across chevrons into his path.
Guildford County Court judge found neither witness credible and dismissed both claim and counterclaim for failure to discharge the burden of proof.
Post-accident conversation in which Crompton told Cooper she had missed the junction was accepted by Cooper in evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from Guildford County Court liability judgment after split trial; appeal by Crompton only, no cross-appeal by Cooper.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; negligence established against Mrs Cooper; judgment entered for Crompton on counterclaim; costs to Crompton.
enrichment.ratio: In road traffic cases it is rare that neither party can discharge the burden of proof where conflicting accounts exist; the judge must analyse available pointers rather than treat the case as Ashraf v Akram exceptional. Immediate post-accident admissions, familiarity with the junction, and vehicle damage may indicate which account is more probable. Where the Court of Appeal can make findings as well as the trial judge and no cross-appeal exists, remittal may be avoided to save disproportionate costs.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge was entitled to dismiss both claim and counterclaim on the civil burden of proof
Which driver's account of the collision at M25 junction 10 was more probable
Whether contributory negligence arose if Crompton's account was accepted
Whether the judge should have raised burden-of-proof disposal with advocates before judgment

enrichment.short_title: Front garden not a public place for bladed article offence; affray conviction upheld
key_facts: Police attended Leroy Roberts' home after a child's emergency call reporting parental fighting on 24 June 2001.
Roberts struggled with Sergeant Rutherford, swung a car tyre at PC Lawrence, was subdued and found with a lock knife in his trouser pocket during search at the station.
The Crown Court convicted him of affray and having a bladed article in a public place; he received concurrent 40-hour community punishment orders.
The trial judge held Roberts' narrow Victorian front garden was a 'public place' because harm could be inflicted on passers-by from the low front wall.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against conviction to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) with leave of the single judge.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction on count 2 (bladed article) quashed as no case to answer; affray conviction upheld; sentence unaffected.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 139(7) Criminal Justice Act 1988, 'public place' means a place to which the public have or are permitted access; a private front garden to which only implied licence visitors such as postmen enter is not a public place (R v Edwards and Roberts). It is wrong to extend 'public place' to private land merely because an occupier could reach from that land to harm passers-by; such construction would absurdly depend on fence height and could extend to rooms overlooking the street.
legal_issues: Whether the defendant's front garden was a public place within section 139(7)
Whether the bladed article ruling caused jury confusion on the affray trespass defence
Whether there was no case to answer on the second count

notes: Interlocutory trial ruling on admissibility of similar fact evidence in IP infringement action.

enrichment.short_title: Mattel v Simba: similar fact copying evidence admissible in Barbie/My Scene design right action
key_facts: Mattel sued Simba-Toys for infringement of community unregistered design right and copyright over alleged copying of the 'My Scene' doll in Simba's 'My Style' range.
Mattel's reply pleaded Simba's long history of copying Mattel doll lines and relied on a 28 June 2002 Paris Commercial Court judgment finding systematic copying and unfair competition.
Simba denied copying and later asserted independent design without knowledge of My Scene; Mattel sought to adduce similar fact evidence a week into trial.
Simba objected at a late stage that the evidence was oppressive, of limited probative value, and would require disproportionate investigation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory ruling during High Court Chancery trial on whether Mattel may adduce similar fact evidence of prior copying by Simba.
enrichment.outcome: Similar fact evidence permitted; objection on oppression and probative value rejected.
enrichment.ratio: Similar fact evidence is admissible in civil cases if logically probative and not oppressive or unfair, provided fair notice is given (Mood Music v De Wolfe). Evidence of a pattern of copying may assist on whether defendants had knowledge and opportunity to copy the specific product, even if habit-of-copying evidence alone has limited probative value on the copying issue itself. Late objection fails where defendants had notice in the reply three weeks earlier, responded with counter-allegations rather than seeking early exclusion, and did not cross-examine or deny the copying history.
legal_issues: Whether Mattel's similar fact evidence of prior copying by Simba should be admitted
Probative value of copying history on independent design and knowledge issues
Whether admission would be oppressive or unfair given late stage of trial
Relevance of the Paris Commercial Court judgment

notes: Supplemental postscript to main judgment [2003] EWHC 2228 (Admin); sets relief, declarations and costs but substantive Art 49 analysis is in the principal judgment.

enrichment.short_title: Watts NHS abroad treatment: supplemental order granting EC declarations and 35% costs
key_facts: Following the principal judgment in R (Watts) v Bedford PCT [2003] EWHC 2228, the court heard argument on 14 October 2003 as to precise relief, costs and permission to appeal.

The claimant sought NHS funding/reimbursement for hip replacement surgery abroad because of NHS waiting times; PCT decisions of November 2002 and February 2003 were held erroneous under Article 49 EC in the main judgment.
The court granted extensive declaratory relief on Article 49 EC and Article 22 of Regulation 1408/71 but dismissed the claim for financial reimbursement.
Permission to apply for judicial review was granted on Community law issues only; human rights and domestic law claims were refused.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplemental judgment on relief, costs and permission to appeal following main judicial review judgment handed down on 1 October 2003.
enrichment.outcome: Declaratory relief granted in twelve numbered declarations; application otherwise dismissed; Secretary of State ordered to pay 35% of claimant's costs; permission to appeal granted to claimant and Secretary of State.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant wins important Community law points on Article 49 EC but fails on reimbursement and other issues, a broad-brush proportional costs order rather than issue-by-issue taxation may fairly reflect partial success; here 35% of costs was appropriate. Declaratory relief is appropriate to crystallise EC law rulings on NHS cross-border treatment, prior authorisation, undue delay, and procedural accessibility. Permission to appeal may be granted where issues are of profound importance to the NHS even if success on appeal is uncertain.
legal_issues: What declaratory relief should follow the principal Article 49 EC ruling
Appropriate costs apportionment between claimant and Secretary of State after partial success
Whether permission to appeal should be granted on Community law issues
Whether published NHS reimbursement procedures comply with Article 49 accessibility requirements
